content:
"The article examines the enduring but flawed concept of the "great man" theory of history, which posits that exceptional individuals with outstanding talent, courage, and charisma single-handedly shape the course of human events through their genius and force of personality. This 19th-century idea, originally promoted by Scottish philosopher Thomas Carlyle, has proven remarkably resilient despite the emergence of egalitarian and Marxist social theories, as well as the "history from below" movement initiated by EP Thompson in the 1960s, which sought to democratize historical narratives.

Carlyle championed figures such as Aristotle, Julius Caesar, Napoleon, Martin Luther, and the prophet Muhammad as towering historical heroes who fundamentally and permanently transformed the world. According to his worldview, ordinary people could only passively observe, marvel at, admire, and obediently follow these elite leaders who ostensibly directed the course of universal history from the top down. The author characterizes this perspective as fundamentally flawed, though acknowledges its enduring appeal and seductive power.

The article notes that this heroic ideal continues to attract adherents, primarily men, who genuinely believe themselves destined for greatness, possessing special missions, sacred callings, or savior-like duties to lead nations and peoples. These individuals possess supreme confidence, believing they possess unique insights and possess sufficient ruthlessness and arrogance to impose their worldviews on entire populations. However, the author contends that in contemporary times, such self-proclaimed "great" men typically function not as heroes in the traditional sense, but rather as anti-heroes or villains, despite wielding considerable power."
